reasons.specificity: The lexicon and paired-usage table track the article's own distinctions—severe style, speculative vs representational thinking, fetishism vs mystification, prehistory vs capital's coming-to-be, and Rose's vs the article's view of Marx—rather than generic Hegel-Marx themes; the F-citation system maps claims to their textual locations with reasonable granularity.
reasons.anchoring: Most anchor quotes appear verbatim in the source and support the stated sense (e.g., 'designed solely to do justice to the integrity of the object,' 'mystiﬁcation marks the forms irrationality takes,' 'The trade is not the prehistory of capital'); one citation gives Marx vol. 3 p. 516 for the 'most fetishized form' quote but the article cites it as Marx 1981: 516 while the analysis header uses 'Marx, 1976: 516,' a mis-citation that does not invent a quote but misattributes the volume—minor but real.
reasons.non_obviousness: The analysis usefully separates fetishism from mystification as distinct operations rather than synonyms, explicates why 'lack of identity' has two scopes (epistemic and socio-historical), and explains why Smallwood's slave-trade argument is not merely additive but reframes the boundary of 'capital' itself—distinctions a casual reader would likely conflate.
reasons.coherence: The F-citation ledger and the two tables use consistent terminology and attribution throughout; the 'voice vs. sense' resolution in the paired-usage table correctly explains the Rose-attribution/article-claim asymmetry rather than treating it as contradiction; the scope-assessment section is consistent with the table claims.
reasons.usefulness: The lexicon covers all central terms with usable columns (sense, contrast, boundary, anchor, consequence) and the paired-usage table addresses the most confusing apparent contradictions in the article; the findings ledger with numbered entries provides a verifiable inventory rather than a summary essay, helping a reader navigate the argument.
reasons.hallucination_risk: No invented external positions or false cross-text comparisons are introduced; the one factual slip—attributing the interest-bearing capital 'most fetishized form' quote to Marx 1976: 516 when the article cites Marx 1981: 516 (vol. 3)—is a transcription error on a detail rather than a fabricated claim; all interpretive warrants are traceable to explicit passages.

decisive_errors.claim: The analysis's F16 anchor truncates the Marx passage as 'the ability of money or a commodity to valorize its own value independent of' and labels it as coming from 'Marx, 1976: 516', repeating a citation error present in the article itself (the article at one point writes 'Marx, 1981: 516' and at another 'Marx, 1976: 516' for the same vol. 3 passage). The analysis inherits rather than corrects this inconsistency.
decisive_errors.counter_passage: The block quote from Capital in the article reads 'the capital mystiﬁcation in the most ﬂagrant form (Marx, 1976: 516)' but the article's footnote 2 also cites 'Marx (1981: 516)' for a related passage; Capital vol. 3 is Marx 1981 in the reference list, not 1976.

score.one_line: A well-structured, source-faithful lexicon that cleanly separates fetishism from mystification and voice-shifts from genuine ambiguity, with one inherited citation-volume error and otherwise strong anchoring.
